title: The Bell at Union Station
author: Lexi Zotomayor
excerpt: Touching a replica of the Liberty Bell outside Washington’s Union Station awakens memories of Philippine church bells, wartime ghosts, and a childhood ice cream cart.
bodyText:
In Philippine towns, where the Spaniards laid out the streets around a central plaza, the church bell was once the only clock anyone needed. It told you when to wake up, when to put down your tools, and when to gather your family before the home altar for the evening Angelus. Growing up there, you learn early that a bell is more than just noise. It keeps time for a whole town.

When I travel, I always end up looking for small reminders of home. That is how I found myself in Washington, D.C.,standing in front of Union Station beside the American Legion Freedom Bell. It looks just like Philadelphia’s Liberty Bell—twice as big, though without the crack. In 1975, it toured the country to help steady the national mood after Watergate.

I am not American by birth, yet I grew up loving the idea of America from afar. Long before high school, I knew the words to the *Star-Spangled Banner* and the Pledge of Allegiance by heart. I picked them up from my father, who read American history the way other men read the morning paper. Standing there in the gray Washington afternoon,watching commuters hurry past, I felt a sudden tightening in my chest.
I stepped closer and laid a hand against the bell’s cool, heavy flank.

You cannot touch one bell without waking up all the others you have ever known. Under the low hum of that bronze,the train station vanished. Suddenly I was back in my childhood. I heard the sharp clang of schoolyards, the deep peals of Sunday mornings, and the cheerful ringing of the neighborhood ice cream man pushing his wooden cart down a dusty street.
And beneath those sounds, rising straight out of my father’s history books, came the ghosts of three other bells.

In 1901, in the town of Balangiga on the island of Samar, the local church bells were rung—not to call people to prayer,but to signal a guerrilla ambush on a garrison of American soldiers. Forty-eight unarmed men died in the morning heat.Furious, the American general ordered his troops to take no prisoners and turn the interior of Samar into a "howling wilderness." When the fighting stopped, the soldiers took the three church bells home as war trophies. They sat on foreign soil for over a century until patient talks finally brought them back to Samar.

A cab horn blared at the curb, snapping me back to Washington. My hand was still resting on the bronze, and all that history had left me with one clear thought: I wanted ice cream. Some habits never leave you, no matter how old you get. I gave the Freedom Bell a polite pat, left the ghosts of Samar and Philadelphia to sort things out in the courtyard,and went inside the station to hunt down a cone.
